justification: Decides whether a council chapter is read from OCR or from a text layer known to be unreadable. The first complete 47-batch run got 44 batches and discarded all of them, re-enqueueing the same garbled text it existed to replace. Every constant corrected here was sized from a warm idle endpoint and is wrong under real load.

pre_impl.existing_data: No database read or write and no schema change. The evidence is one complete run of city_of_sydney/section-3-general-provisions against the live Modal endpoint, 141 pages in 47 batches, 2026-09-19.
pre_impl.assumption_mismatch: Three constants were sized from a warm idle endpoint. Measured across the 44 batches that responded: min 68s, median 104s, p90 118s, max 140s — against OCR_READ_TIMEOUT of 120s, so the cap sat AT the p90 with batches landing at 118, 118, 119, 119 and 120 seconds. The 85.3s that justified a 3-page batch was a single warm measurement; under 47 sustained requests the median is 22 percent slower and the tail reaches 140s. Separately, a whole-chapter retry budget of 6 was consumed by batches 11 and 15 taking two each, leaving two for batch 45 — a constant that cannot cover 47 batches, the same error as a fixed 600s OCR deadline and a fixed 1200s process cap. Finally the all-or-nothing rule then discarded 138 good pages.
pre_impl.new_vs_existing: Changes only how long one batch may be silent, how many retries a chapter may spend, and what happens to the pages of a batch that never succeeds. A healthy run is unchanged: one call per batch, no failed pages, same output.
pre_impl.external_source_error: This is entirely about an external source failing. Every failure still fails closed in the direction that matters — a chapter whose OCR is mostly missing is abandoned to its text layer rather than served as a patchwork, and a dead endpoint is now detected within a few batches instead of at the end of the chapter.
pre_impl.frontend_type: No API or component change. This runs in the nightly extractor.
pre_impl.user_failure_mode: Two directions, and the previous design was wrong about which was safer. Too strict and 138 good pages are thrown away for 3 bad ones, which is what happened and which re-served unreadable text. Too loose and a chapter becomes mostly text layer with OCR sprinkled through it, which is harder to reason about than a clean fallback — so a share cap abandons the chapter past 10 percent of pages, checked as each batch fails rather than only at the end.

falsifiable_check.fails_when: The silence cap drops back to or below the observed 140s tail, or rises so far it stops detecting a dead endpoint; the batch size and the cap stop being sized against each other; the retry budget goes flat again, drops below the floor for a small chapter, or grows toward one retry per batch; a failed batch discards the whole chapter again; an empty OCR entry blanks a page instead of falling back to its text layer; the failed-page share cap is loosened; or the share is checked only at the end, so a dead endpoint costs the whole chapter to discover. The connection is not re-established between the PDF work and the first query after it; the cursor is not re-made from the revived connection; main stops reviving its own; liveness is decided by conn.closed rather than by executing; or the replacement connection drops the keepalives.
falsifiable_check.observed_red: Ten mutations planted, ten CAUGHT. Five on the tuning: restoring the 120s cap, flattening the retry budget, removing the early abort, blanking a page instead of falling back, and loosening the share cap to 90 percent. Five on the connection: removing the revive from extract_chapter, reviving but keeping the stale cursor, leaving main's connection dead, trusting conn.closed instead of pinging, and reconnecting without keepalives. 12 new tests, 47 across the three affected files, 386 across every related suite. Two existing tests failed honestly when the fallback changed from all-or-nothing to per-page and were rewritten to the new contract rather than deleted — and one of those failures found a real regression: without an early share check, a dead endpoint cost 16 calls to learn what the first three batches already said.

functions.name: ocr_chapter_retry_budget
functions.input: The number of batches the chapter will be split into.
functions.output: The retries the whole chapter may spend: a quarter of the batches, never fewer than the floor of 6.
functions.if_none: A small chapter keeps exactly the floor it had, so nothing gets stingier. The result is always well under half the batch count, so a dead endpoint cannot spend the run retrying.

functions.name: fetch_ocr_page_texts
functions.input: A chapter PDF path and its page count.
functions.output: Per-page texts, with an empty string for any page whose batch never succeeded — the marker that page keeps its text layer. None when too many pages failed, or the budget ran out.
functions.if_none: The caller stays on the text layer for the whole chapter, as before. What changed is that this is now reserved for a chapter that is mostly unreadable, rather than triggered by a single bad batch.

functions.name: DcpExtractor._page_text
functions.input: A pdfplumber page object and its 1-based page number within the chapter PDF.
functions.output: The OCR text for that page, or the text layer when the OCR entry is empty.
functions.if_none: An empty OCR entry means that page's batch failed, so it falls through to the text layer it would have had anyway. Returning the empty string would silently blank a page the reader can still partly use — worse than the defect being worked around. A genuinely blank page falls through to an equally blank text layer, so nothing is lost.

functions.name: revive
functions.input: The batch connection, after it has sat idle through roughly an hour of PDF work in a child process.
functions.output: The same connection when it still answers a SELECT 1, otherwise a fresh one with the same keepalive settings, with the dead one closed rather than leaked.
functions.if_none: There is no None case: it always returns a usable connection or raises from psycopg2.connect, which the caller already handles as a chapter failure. A close that itself fails is swallowed, because losing the reconnect to its own cleanup would be the same lost hour one layer along.

values.name: OCR_READ_TIMEOUT = 300
values.value: Seconds of silence before a batch is abandoned, raised from 120
values.why: 120 sat at the p90 of the real distribution, which is a coin flip rather than a margin. 300 is over twice the worst observed batch and still calls a dead endpoint within five minutes, which is what this cap is actually for. Total duration is bounded by the chapter budget, not by this.
values.source: Measured across 44 responding batches of a 47-batch run, 2026-09-19: min 68s, median 104s, p90 118s, max 140s, with batches landing at 118, 118, 119, 119 and 120 seconds.
values.if_missing: At 120 roughly one batch in ten dies on a slow container, and on a 47-batch chapter that is several failures per run.

values.name: the retry budget is a share of the batches
values.why: A fixed 6 cannot cover 47 batches. On the run that prompted this, batches 11 and 15 took two retries each and batch 45 was left with two, ran out, and cost the chapter its 138 good pages. A quarter tolerates a genuinely flaky endpoint while staying far below retrying everything.
values.source: The same run: three batches failed, two were rescued, the third exhausted the budget.
values.if_missing: Flat again and a long chapter loses to the third transient blip; unbounded and a dead endpoint spends the wall-clock proving it is dead.

values.name: OCR_MAX_FAILED_PAGE_FRACTION = 0.10
values.value: The share of pages that may fall back before the chapter is abandoned
values.why: Keeping 138 of 141 OCR pages is plainly better than keeping none, which is what all-or-nothing actually did. But a chapter that is mostly text layer with OCR sprinkled through it is harder to reason about than a clean fallback, so there has to be a line. It is checked as each batch fails, not only at the end, or a dead endpoint is discovered one batch at a time across the whole chapter.
values.source: Measured: without the early check a 20-batch chapter cost 16 calls to learn what the first three said.
values.if_missing: Loosened, a chapter of almost entirely garbled text is served as though OCR succeeded. Removed from the loop, a dead endpoint costs the whole chapter to detect.

values.name: a SELECT 1 ping, not conn.closed
values.why: psycopg2's conn.closed reports what THIS process did to the connection, not what the server did, so it still reads open on a connection the pooler has already dropped. Executing something is the only way to find out. Keepalives are kept as well rather than replaced: they still cover the idle socket reap they were added for, they simply cannot cover a pooler closing the session.
values.source: Measured on two complete runs that died at diff_provisions with 'server closed the connection unexpectedly' — the fourth carried keepalives and died identically, which is what disproved the idle-reap theory.
values.if_missing: An hour of correct work is discarded at the last step. The fourth run produced OCR for all 141 pages and extracted 94 sections before losing it.

queries.purpose: Decide which text each page contributes to the provisions the extractor later writes: the OCR read, or the page's own text layer.
queries.where_clause: Not applicable: no query is added or changed, and the rows those queries later write differ only in carrying OCR text rather than a garbled text layer.

break_it.scenario: The silence cap is lowered again, or the batch size raised, so batches sit back inside the tail of the duration distribution.
break_it.what_happens: Roughly one batch in ten dies on a slow container, which on a 47-batch chapter is several failures a run — and before the per-page fallback that meant losing the chapter.
break_it.how: Tests assert the cap clears the worst observed batch with room, and that the batch size times the measured under-load per-page cost still fits inside it, so the two cannot drift apart.

break_it.scenario: The cap is raised without limit to stop failures entirely.
break_it.what_happens: A genuinely dead endpoint stops being detected and holds the nightly extraction open.
break_it.how: A ceiling is asserted as a confusable negative: this cap exists to notice silence, and total duration is bounded by the chapter budget instead.

break_it.scenario: A page whose batch failed is served blank instead of falling back.
break_it.what_happens: The empty-string marker is read as 'this page is blank' rather than 'use the text layer', silently deleting text the reader could still partly use — worse than the defect being worked around.
break_it.how: _page_text falls through when the OCR entry is empty. This was NOT the original behaviour: it returned the entry unconditionally, and the per-page design would have blanked those pages. Found by checking the claim rather than asserting it, and pinned by a test.

break_it.scenario: The text handed to the extractor is OCR for most pages and text layer for a few, and nothing downstream can tell which is which.
break_it.what_happens: A provision assembled across a batch boundary mixes a clean OCR page with a garbled one, so a single clause reads half correctly — harder to spot than a wholly unreadable chapter, and it reaches the same queries and the same review queue.
break_it.how: The share cap keeps this to under a tenth of pages, and the failed page numbers are printed so the boundary is visible in the run log. Beyond that the judgement is deliberately made at the write rather than here: the legibility guard merged in #1141 compares the committed result against what is live and refuses a chapter that comes out less readable, whichever pages caused it.

break_it.scenario: A dead endpoint is discovered one batch at a time.
break_it.what_happens: Every batch is attempted and retried before the chapter is abandoned, so learning the endpoint is broken costs the whole chapter's wall-clock.
break_it.how: The failed-page share is checked as each batch fails, not only at the end. This regression was introduced BY the per-page fallback and caught by an existing test, which measured 16 calls where three sufficed.

break_it.scenario: A chapter is served as a patchwork of OCR and garbled text layer.
break_it.what_happens: Most pages read correctly and a minority are nonsense, which is harder to spot and reason about than a chapter that is uniformly one or the other.
break_it.how: Past 10 percent of pages the chapter is abandoned to its text layer. Below that, the legibility guard merged in #1141 independently refuses the commit if the result is less readable than what is already live, so the judgement is made against the actual outcome at the write.

break_it.scenario: The endpoint degrades further under longer runs than the one measured.
break_it.what_happens: A 122-batch chapter (city_of_sydney section 5) may show a worse tail than the 47-batch run these numbers come from, and batches start failing again.
break_it.how: Not addressed, and not knowable from this run. 300s is over twice the worst batch seen at 47, but the distribution under 122 sequential requests has not been measured. The per-page fallback and the share cap mean the consequence is now a partial or clean fallback rather than a lost chapter, which is the point.
break_it.repro: Run the extractor on city_of_sydney/section-5-specific-areas and compare the batch-duration distribution.

break_it.scenario: This is taken to mean the chapter now re-extracts successfully.
break_it.what_happens: It has not yet. Two runs have failed, for different reasons each time.
break_it.how: Not claimed. These corrections come from the second run; the third has not completed at the time of writing, and the honest position is that the mechanism is now sized against measured behaviour rather than proven to finish.

break_it.scenario: The connection is revived inside extract_chapter but main keeps holding the dead one.
break_it.what_happens: The first chapter's hour of PDF work leaves every later chapter in the batch with a corpse, and the run summary and registry updates fail too — so a multi-chapter night dies after the first chapter regardless of how well the rest extract.
break_it.how: extract_chapter takes conn as a parameter, so its rebinding cannot reach main's. main revives its own around each call, and a test asserts that by reading the loop.

post_merge.db_reset: No. Nothing is written by this change.
post_merge.manual_verify: Yes: re-run city_of_sydney/section-3. The fourth run produced OCR for all 141 pages and extracted 94 sections before losing it to the dead connection, so the OCR side is demonstrated and the write side is not. Four runs have now failed for four different reasons.
